prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength lattice for neutral atoms to systematic uncertainty and stability at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks (B061, Katori and Ye) as a single-part prize. The scientific case has not weakened under challenge. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a specific, checkable idea that removes Doppler and recoil shifts for a large neutral-atom ensemble while cancelling the light shift to first order, and Ye's group demonstrated 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and stability and the many-body clock regime. The claim is exact and measured, not open to reinterpretation. Independent laboratories reproduce the performance and compare clocks across institutes, and the payoff is already realised in millimetre-scale redshift tests, bounds on varying constants and the basis for redefining the second. Several colleagues who do not share my field, and who moved to this position after reading the openings, reach it from the attribution and maturity side. I note Pearce's request, and I agree it should be on the record, that my Hall-laboratory lineage might bias me. I have therefore tried to test B061 against B013 on the same criteria (definiteness of the discovery, maturity, exactness of credit) rather than on the count, and on those criteria B061 still comes out ahead for this year, though not by a wide margin.
statement.case_against: I take the strongest objections seriously. First, the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-quantum-system control sit next to this work, and a sceptic can call it a successor refinement of recognised metrology. I do not think the objection is decisive, because the lattice clock is a different physical route (many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength trap rather than a single ion), but a committee that wants a prize opening a new regime of nature rather than a new level of measurement could reasonably prefer B013. Second, the credit is not free of dispute: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and the ion-clock community have claims that two names leave out, and Olsson's question whether the 10^-18 milestones belong to Ye alone or to a wider group is fair. Third, the second has not been redefined, so the practical culmination is still ahead. Against my own preference, the field-opening breadth of moire quantum matter is real.

responses.point: Danielsson argues for B013 as the discovery in which a quantitative prediction was followed by a new regime of correlated matter, argues that the unresolved pairing mechanism concerns follow-on physics, and says that ease of attribution should not decide the ranking.
responses.response: I accept that last point as a matter of principle: I do not rank B061 first because its credit is tidy, and I do not want the committee to treat tidy credit as a substitute for scientific weight. My reasons are that the claim is definite, reproduced and mature, and that its attribution is a consequence of that, not the reason for it. I also concede, as you and Eriksson argue, that the open pairing mechanism is a citation-wording issue and does not threaten the existence of the flat-band platform. Where I still differ is on the question the chair has put: the B013 credit set is not merely incomplete at the margin, since Cao and Fatemi carried the 2018 experiments, and a three-name cap cannot repair that. A citation that has to say openly which contributions it honours and which it does not is a weaker public position than a pair that covers the decisive concept and the decisive demonstration. I have not changed my configuration, but I would not regard B013 as a mistake.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B013 after the opening, grants that Katori and Ye is the cleanest attribution, but says the pending redefinition of the second means the practical culmination is still ahead and that the clocks are not more novel than the moire platform.
responses.response: We agree on the facts and differ in weighting, as you say. On the redefinition, I would separate the scientific discovery from its institutional adoption: the 10^-18 performance and the cross-laboratory comparisons are already in hand, and the vote of the metrology community on the second does not add to or subtract from that. A prize for the clock does not require waiting for the redefinition, though I accept that waiting would lose little if the committee preferred it. On novelty, I will not claim the clock opens a new regime of matter. My claim is narrower: it is a new instrument and a new level of control of a many-atom system, with a settled result. I would ask you the same question you asked of me, whether on your criteria the nature of the correlated states in magic-angle graphene, which you yourself call incomplete, is sufficiently settled to write a citation this year.

responses.point: Pearce supports B061 and the narrow two-name credit, rejects the 2012 precedent as a weakness, and asks that my disclosed Hall-laboratory lineage be noted in the record when my ranking is weighed.
responses.response: I agree that the disclosure should be on the record, and I have restated it in my conflict note. I also agree that the 2012 prize concerned individual quantum systems and does not cover the neutral-atom lattice. Your point that Lindroth reaches the same ranking without any such tie is fair, but I would not lean on it too hard, since Lindroth and I are both atomic physicists and share a field bias that is not a conflict of interest but should be tested. That is why I have checked B061 against B013 above on common criteria. On the narrow citation question put by the chair, I would word the citation on the optical lattice clock and neutral-atom precision, with no statement on ion-clock priority, and I would have it name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 milestone.

responses.point: Johansson holds B034 first on conceptual originality and clean credit, and argues that the overlap objection against B061 with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the same objection that is raised against Cirac and Zoller.
responses.response: That symmetry argument is a fair challenge and I do not want to treat the two cases differently on the same grounds. The way I draw the line is by the novelty of the physical idea. The 2012 prize recognised experimental control of single ions and photons, and the experiments realising the Cirac-Zoller gate belong to that tradition, whereas the lattice clock is a different platform and a different route to accuracy. You answer that the 2012 prize did not honour the theoretical proposals, which is correct, and I have moved on this: I no longer say the overlap alone excludes B034, and I keep it as my second alternative. But a theory-only prize leaves out Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and the other experimentalists who made the proposals real, and the simulation half is still producing its first results beyond classical reach, so I continue to think B034 is better after the experimental record matures.

uncertainties: Whether a committee that weights discovery of a new regime of nature over precision measurement would, on reflection, place B013 first; this is a disagreement on weighting that evidence will not resolve.

How much the claims of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and of ion-clock pioneers, should shape the citation wording given that the three-name cap leaves two names credited.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes B061 a stronger candidate next year than this year, or whether recognising a demonstrated 10^-18 capability now loses nothing.
How much my own field proximity and the Hall-laboratory lineage are biasing my judgement of B061 against B013, which I have tried to correct by applying the same criteria to both.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I trained under Sune Svanberg at Lund and spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; the lattice-clock field descends partly from that precision laser-spectroscopy tradition, as Pearce and Lindroth asked to have recorded. It is a scientific lineage and not a collaboration or shared institution with Katori or Ye, and I have found no documented tie to any credited name, so no recusal is required. Separately, I work on rare-earth-ion quantum memories with European collaborators and took part in WACQT management, which touches B002 and the quantum-information candidates (B034, B018) more than B061; none of them is in my preferred configuration.
